clue.text: Finally enjoy prize after good turn

indicators.note: takes only the final letter of the next word

parts.note: to prize something is to rate it highly

explanation.surface: Someone does a good turn and finally gets to enjoy a prize for it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good turn' reads as a kind deed, but good is only G and turn is the definition. 'After' puts G first, so the order is G, then Y, then RATE.
explanation.definitionFit: To gyrate is to turn or spin round and round.

clue.text: Leave a fitness class, finding yourself off the deep end

definitions.note: 'Going ape' is a verb phrase; 'finding yourself off the deep end' is the sense it replaces.

parts.note: a going is a leaving, a departure
PE = physical education, the school gym lesson

explanation.surface: Someone walks out of a gym class, feeling out of their depth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off the deep end' sounds like a swimming lesson, which suits the fitness class, but here it means losing your temper or going mad.
explanation.definitionFit: Going ape and going off the deep end both mean losing control in anger or excitement.

clue.text: One with a compass — point's lost by him?

definitions.meaning: a hiker navigating the countryside by compass
not a compass point but the point of a story, which a long-winded talker loses

explanation.surface: A hiker with a compass somehow still loses his way to the next point.
explanation.walkthrough: The compass makes 'point' look like a compass point; a RAMBLER is both a country walker and someone who talks on without getting to the point.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers two people at once: the hiker with a map and compass, and the digressive talker.

clue.text: Drink the writer raised, it honours a family

parts.note: a tot is a small drink, usually of spirits

indicators.note: in a down clue raised means the word is turned upwards, so it reads backwards

parts.note: the writer refers to the setter, who is me

explanation.surface: Someone raises a glass to a family emblem in a toast.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma hides the join: the definition is the closing phrase, describing a carved pole or emblem, not the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is a natural object or animal adopted as the emblem of a clan, honoured as a symbol of the kin group.

clue.text: Perhaps clubs holding all that remains: hands seen at ends of these?

definitions.text: hands seen at ends of these?

indicators.note: the first word holds the second inside it

parts.note: clubs are an example of arms, weapons; 'perhaps' flags the example

explanation.surface: A card player asks whether all that is left in the hand is clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: Clubs, hands and remains all point to a card game; clubs are in fact weapons. Your hands rest at the ends of a chair's armrests.
explanation.definitionFit: Armrests are the arms of a chair, where your hands lie at the far end.

clue.text: Looked back on scripture lessons: cool!

parts.note: RE = religious education, the school subject

explanation.surface: Someone thinks back fondly on their old scripture classes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cool!' reads as a schoolchild's exclamation, but it is an adjective meaning calm. RE is the British school subject Religious Education.
explanation.definitionFit: To recollect something is to remember it, to look back on it.

clue.text: Copy badly executed procedure

indicators.note: something carried out badly comes out jumbled

explanation.surface: A botched procedure produced a poor copy.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram indicator sits between definition and fodder and reads naturally as describing the procedure.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to make a duplicate of a picture or document.

clue.text: Part of Croatian city on high

parts.note: Split is a port on the Croatian coast

explanation.surface: A travel note about a hilltop quarter of a Croatian city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Part' looks like a noun, a district of the city, but it is the verb: to part is to separate.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for the verb: to separate, as a couple ending a relationship does.

clue.text: Hunts, in scrubs

definitions.meaning: to scour an area is to search it thoroughly
to scour a pan is to scrub it

explanation.surface: Someone searches, dressed in hospital scrubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scrubs' reads as the clothes surgeons wear; here it is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Scour means both to search hard and to scrub clean.

clue.text: Section of certain material one may wish to escape

indicators.note: the answer is a section cut from the words that follow

explanation.surface: Some cloth or text you would rather get away from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One may wish to escape' reads as describing the material; it is a person who wants to break out.
explanation.definitionFit: An inmate is a prisoner, someone who may wish to escape.

clue.text: Somewhere in Mexico, a Catholic by cupola, trembling

indicators.note: trembling suggests the letters are shaken about, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Mexican churchgoer stands beside a dome shaken by an earthquake.
explanation.walkthrough: Mix A, C and CUPOLA together; the trembling fits a country known for earthquakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Acapulco is a Pacific resort city in the Mexican state of Guerrero, so it is a place in that country.

clue.text: Good old crossword setter: lad's flipping getting top award

parts.note: the setter of this crossword is Everyman, who refers to himself as me

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the word is read back to front

parts.note: the lad's 's is 'is', a link; the word itself is used

explanation.surface: Proud praise for a veteran puzzle-setter and a boy who wins first prize, perhaps at gymnastics with all that flipping.
explanation.walkthrough: Everyman refers to himself in the first person, so 'crossword setter' gives the pronoun a setter would use for himself.
explanation.definitionFit: First place at the Olympics and similar contests is rewarded with this prize, the highest honour available.

clue.text: Casting out money and Red Book

indicators.note: casting metal reshapes it, so the letters are remoulded

explanation.surface: Someone throws out cash along with a little red book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Casting out' looks like a phrase meaning throwing away; only 'Casting' is the indicator and 'out' is fodder. Red Book is a decoy for Mao's Little Red Book.
explanation.definitionFit: Deuteronomy is the fifth book of the Old Testament.

clue.text: River creature getting closer in Cockney's game

indicators.note: the word as a Cockney would say it while playing; a Cockney speaker traditionally drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: in the children's game of hot and cold, a seeker who is getting closer is told they are getting hotter

explanation.surface: A Londoner's game of hunting for a riverside animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In ... game' points to the hunting game 'hot and cold', where getting closer is HOTTER; 'Cockney's' version drops the H. Cockneys are working-class East Londoners famous for dropping H sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: Otters are semi-aquatic mammals that live along rivers and hunt fish there.

clue.text: Leisure activity from which you may hope to be dropped?

definitions.meaning: a hobby or pastime, taken at face value

definitions.text: from which you may hope to be dropped?
definitions.meaning: surface: a hobby so dull you want to be thrown out of it; setter: something you are literally dropped from, an aircraft

explanation.surface: A hobby so dull you would rather be kicked out of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dropped' suggests being thrown out of a group or team; skydivers are dropped from the plane, and they very much hope to be.
explanation.definitionFit: The sport is a leisure pursuit whose whole point is being dropped from a height.

clue.text: Punch a tenor, getting personal in area with many restaurants

parts.note: to chin someone is to punch them on the jaw
T = tenor, as in SATB choir parts
your own = personal to you; 'getting' just adds it on

explanation.surface: A brawl breaks out when someone punches a tenor in a restaurant district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting personal' reads as a fight turning nasty, but it just adds OWN. Chin as a verb, to hit on the chin, is informal British.
explanation.definitionFit: A Chinatown is a city's Chinese quarter, known for its many restaurants.

clue.text: Those intoning M-A-G-I-C?

definitions.meaning: people chanting, as a wizard chants an incantation
the hyphens show the word said letter by letter; 'magic' tempts you towards casting spells

explanation.surface: Wizards chanting magic words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intoning magic' suggests wizards chanting spells; the hyphens show someone simply spelling out a word letter by letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Spellers are people who spell out words, letter by letter.

clue.text: Esther shortly dons formal footwear, makes timely investment

indicators.note: dons means puts on, so the clothing word goes around the name

parts.note: prim means stiffly formal and proper
a pump is a light shoe, such as a court shoe or plimsoll

indicators.note: shortly means cut short, so the name loses its last letter

explanation.surface: A woman called Esther puts on prim, smart shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'dons' picture is literal: the shortened name is dressed in the two outer words, one each side, as if wearing them. A pump here is a light dancing shoe, not a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: To prime the pump is an idiom for putting money in early to stimulate growth, like pouring water to start a pump.

clue.text: Grandeur that is retrograde, Everyman's a tragic relic of former times

definitions.text: a tragic relic of former times

parts.note: pomp is ceremonial grandeur and splendour

indicators.note: retrograde means moving backwards, so the letters are read in reverse

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is
Everyman is the setter, who would call himself I

explanation.surface: The setter reflects on the faded grandeur of a tragic ruin from antiquity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrograde' turns IE into EI; then I for the setter finishes it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Roman town buried by Vesuvius in AD 79 survives as ruins, a tragic remnant of the ancient world.

clue.text: Perfect, working out pain

indicators.note: letters put to work are moved into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Exercising away your pain is perfect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Working out' reads as exercise, but only 'working' is the indicator and 'out' is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Utopian describes an ideal, perfect state.

clue.text: Ancient Greece's artisanal trinkets' expensive stones, primarily?

definitions.text: Ancient Greece's artisanal trinkets' expensive stones, primarily?

indicators.note: take the primary, first, letter of each word

explanation.surface: A museum label on the precious stones in ancient Greek craftwork.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does both jobs: its initials spell the answer, and agates were indeed used in ancient Greek jewellery.
explanation.definitionFit: Agates are semi-precious banded stones used in ancient jewellery and carvings.

clue.text: After a month, publication rejected letter from Athens

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so all the letters are read backwards
After places the publication behind a and the month before everything is turned

parts.note: a mag, short for magazine, is a publication

explanation.surface: A magazine turns down a submission after a month, sent by a Greek correspondent.
explanation.walkthrough: AM followed by MAG makes AMMAG, which 'rejected' turns round. 'letter from Athens' looks like correspondence; it is a Greek letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamma is the third letter of the Greek alphabet, used in Athens.

clue.text: Traditionalists hold out with loco beliefs in the end

indicators.note: letters that are out are out of order
takes only the end letter of beliefs

explanation.surface: Conservatives stubbornly cling to their crazy beliefs until the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hold out' reads as a phrase for resisting, but 'out' is the anagram indicator acting on HOLD, LOCO and the S.
explanation.definitionFit: The old school are those who keep to traditional ways.

clue.text: Bird that's seen on building site

explanation.surface: A bird spotted on a construction site.
explanation.walkthrough: It reads as one bird in one place; it is two different cranes.
explanation.definitionFit: A crane is both a wading bird and a tall lifting machine on building sites.

clue.text: English books thrice rejected, embroiling English again in confrontation

indicators.note: sent back, so written backwards

parts.note: OT = Old Testament books, three times

explanation.surface: An English literature row over three rejected books turns into a face-off.
explanation.walkthrough: E plus OT three times, reversed, makes TOTOTOE; the second E goes in after the first TO.
explanation.definitionFit: Toe-to-toe means standing face to face in direct confrontation.

clue.text: Dog tooth

definitions.meaning: the adjective for dogs, also used as a noun for one

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dog tooth' reads as one thing, even a fabric pattern, but it is two separate definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A canine is a dog, and also the pointed tooth beside the incisors.

clue.text: Secret agent's drinking in pub by Earl's woodland

indicators.note: drinking in means taking inside, so the spy word holds the pub and the earl

parts.note: a spy is a secret agent, so the possessive gives spys

explanation.surface: A spy having a drink in a pub beside an earl's estate woods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drinking in' means taking in, the containment signal; 'woodland' covers several small woods.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinney is a small wood or copse, so spinneys are areas of woodland.

clue.text: Plays safe in t-shirts, to some extent

indicators.note: only part of the words is used

explanation.surface: Someone takes no risks by staying in t-shirts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plays safe' reads as one phrase, but 'Plays' alone is the definition, in the sense of a feint or dummy move in sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Feints are deceptive moves or plays in fencing, boxing or football.
